entries.title: Karak Chai
entries.excerpt: Karak chai is a strong, sweet milk tea of CTC black tea, evaporated milk and cardamom, born in the 1960s Gulf and now a global cafe category growing at double digits.

content.text: Karak chai is a strong, sweet milk tea built on CTC black tea, evaporated milk, sugar and cardamom, boiled down to a dense, caramel-toned emulsion. The name comes from the Hindi word for strong, and the drink was born in the 1960s Gulf, where South Asian chaiwallas adapted masala chai to local supply chains.

Today karak is a category, not a curiosity: the unofficial national drink of Qatar, a daily drive-thru ritual across the UAE, and a fast-growing menu line in London, Toronto and New York. Qatar's tea market alone is compounding at 11.6% a year.
For operators the challenge is replication: authentic karak takes 15-20 minutes of attended boiling. A commercial karak base delivers the same profile in 30 seconds.

entries.title: Ticket Time
entries.excerpt: Ticket time is the gap between order and handoff. Drive-thru coffee benchmarks sit near 40 seconds, and every manual prep step on the bar pushes the number up.

content.text: Ticket time is the interval between the moment an order is placed and the moment it is handed to the guest. In specialty coffee the drive-thru benchmark sits around 40 seconds, and queue research shows customers abandoning lines after five to seven minutes.

Every additional preparation step on the bar stretches the number: measuring cream, scaling two sugars, boiling tea. A scratch karak runs 15-20 minutes; a scratch raf stacks up to roughly 115 seconds of manual steps. Both collapse under a morning rush.
Soluble bases compress the sequence to dose, steam, serve: 20-30 seconds per cup regardless of who is behind the machine.
Read more: Raf Coffee Is Ready to Go Global. Its Recipe Is Not
Related terms: Premix, Brix, Encapsulation

entries.title: Encapsulation
entries.excerpt: Encapsulation locks volatile aromatics and fats inside a stable carrier matrix that releases on contact with hot liquid. It is how dry bases keep a fresh-brewed flavor for months.

content.text: Encapsulation is a food-science technique that locks volatile aromatics, fats and other fragile compounds inside a stable carrier matrix, usually during spray drying. The payload stays protected through months of ambient storage and releases only on contact with hot liquid.

For beverage operators this is the mechanism that turns a perishable flavor profile into a dry, shelf-stable SKU. Cardamom top notes, dairy caramel tones and vanilla aromatics survive 18 months in a doypack instead of fading on a hot plate within an hour.
The Base uses encapsulation across its soluble bases so the cup tastes freshly brewed at the moment of preparation, not at the moment of production.

entries.title: Volatile Terpenes
entries.excerpt: Volatile terpenes are the light aromatic compounds behind cardamom and spice top notes. They flash off under heat, which is why held beverages lose aroma within the hour.

content.text: Volatile terpenes are light aromatic compounds, such as cardamom's cineole and terpinyl acetate, that give spiced beverages their top notes. Being volatile, they evaporate rapidly under heat, which makes them the first casualty of long simmering and hot holding.

On a scratch bar this is the mechanism behind fading aroma: a batch brewed at 9 AM smells noticeably flatter by 10:30. In sensory audits, hot-held spiced tea retains roughly 41-78% of key terpenes, while an encapsulated dry matrix holds about 96% until the moment the cup is made.
Stabilizing these compounds at the factory is what lets a soluble base taste freshly spiced at every location, on every shift.
Read more: The Karak Tea Profit Playbook for HoReCa Operators
Related terms: Encapsulation, CTC Tea, Brix

entries.title: CTC Tea
entries.excerpt: CTC (crush, tear, curl) is a black tea process producing dense pellets that extract fast and tannic. It is the standard leaf behind karak and masala chai.

content.text: CTC stands for crush, tear, curl: a black tea process where leaves are shredded and rolled into dense pellets instead of being left whole. The result is a fast-extracting, highly tannic liquor that stands up to milk, sugar and spices.

CTC grades are the backbone of karak and masala chai across the Gulf and South Asia. The trade-off is a narrow extraction window: under-brewed it tastes thin, over-boiled it turns harshly bitter, and that window shifts with water, batch and operator.
The Base fixes CTC extraction at the factory, capturing the full tannic backbone in a soluble base with no boil time on the bar.
Read more: The Karak Tea Profit Playbook for HoReCa Operators
Related terms: Karak Chai, Brix, Premix

entries.title: Brix
entries.excerpt: Brix (°Bx) measures dissolved solids, mostly sugars, in a beverage. It defines sweetness intensity and flavor balance, and locking it is the core of drink standardization.

content.text: Brix (°Bx) measures dissolved solids in a liquid, primarily sugars, expressed as grams per 100 grams of solution. In beverage work it defines sweetness intensity: most sweet drinks land between 8 and 14 °Bx, and that number shapes how the entire flavor system reads in the cup.

A one-point Brix swing changes how tannins, dairy and aromatics balance on the palate. Bars that dose sugar by hand routinely drift two points or more between shifts, and regular customers taste that drift as inconsistency.
Pre-formulated soluble bases lock Brix at the formulation bench. Every location pours the same cup at the same sweetness, with zero scale work on the bar.
Read more: The Karak Tea Profit Playbook for HoReCa Operators
Related terms: CTC Tea, Premix, Encapsulation

entries.title: OEM
entries.excerpt: OEM means a factory manufactures a product to your exact recipe and spec, and you sell it under your brand. Capacity from the plant, formula and market ownership from you.

content.text: OEM, original equipment manufacturing, means a factory produces goods to the buyer's exact specification and recipe, and the buyer sells them under its own brand. The manufacturer supplies capacity and process control; the brand owns the formula and the market.

For beverage operators OEM is the route to a signature product line without building a plant. There is no production CapEx, time to market shrinks from years to months, and batch consistency is handled by a specialist facility. The trade-off: you bring or co-develop the recipe yourself.
The Base runs OEM projects from its Dubai facility, converting customer recipes into shelf-stable soluble beverage systems with fixed cup cost.

entries.excerpt: ODM means the manufacturer both develops the formula and produces the product you brand as your own. The fastest route to market when you have no in-house R&D lab.

content.text: ODM, original design manufacturing, means the factory both develops the formulation and produces the finished product, which the customer sells under its own brand. Unlike OEM, the R&D burden sits with the manufacturer: the customer selects a ready formula or adapts one to taste.

It is the fastest route to market for operators without an in-house lab. You sample catalog formulas, adjust sweetness, dairy character or aromatics, approve the profile and print your brand. MOQ and exclusivity terms become the key negotiating points.
The Base's catalog of soluble bases, from karak to matcha to raf, is built for ODM work: proven recipes adapted and branded as yours.

entries.excerpt: A premix is a pre-blended dry system holding every non-water ingredient of a drink in fixed ratios. One dose plus hot liquid reproduces the recipe identically every time.

content.text: A premix is a pre-blended dry system that combines every non-water ingredient of a drink, dairy solids, sugars, flavors and stabilizers, in fixed ratios inside one package. One measured dose plus hot water or milk reproduces the full recipe, cup after cup.

On the bar a premix deletes multi-ingredient dosing entirely. Brix, dairy character and aromatics are locked at the factory, ticket time drops to roughly 30 seconds, and the storeroom carries one ambient SKU instead of a refrigerated stack.
